script: "She walked in, and the whole thrift store turned into a nightmare.". I walked into the thrift store on a Friday, feeling the usual late‑afternoon buzz of people rummaging through junk. The shelves were a chaotic mix of donated stuff from every corner of the city, and I was the one keeping the prices straight. I had a list, a spreadsheet, a mental map of what everything was worth. I'd already sold a $25 lamp for $5 because the lady was "down on her luck," so I was used to cutting deals. She came in the next minute, all blonde hair and a Lily Pulitzer shirt that looked like it was made for colorblind people. The expression on her face was already pissed. She stormed straight to the art and decor section, grabbed a table lamp, and marched to the register like she owned the place. "How much is this?" she demanded. I looked at the tag: $5.60 plus tax. That price had been set a long time ago, and I was too lazy to change it. "$5.60, plus tax," I said, trying to keep it calm. She scoffed, "Someone sold me one for a dollar less a month ago. We need to be more consistent with our prices." I froze for a second. I remembered that month‑ago visit. I'd sold her a different lamp for $5.60, then lowered the price when she begged. I hadn't corrected her because the store was about to close and I wanted to leave. I figured, "Sure, $5.60, why not?" I punched the price into our old computer system. With tax it was $4.96. She handed me a $50 bill. I handed her $45 in change, grabbed a pen I'd dropped, and she counted it out loud. "What the hell? You said $4.60!" she yelled. I tried to explain sales tax, but she was already mocking me. "So I am supposed to believe that it came out to exactly five dollars? Sure, Jan." Her voice was high and valley‑girl for a second, like a Regina George impression from Mean Girls. I told her the total was $4.96 and that we were short on pennies—our sign said we only had nickels. I offered to find four pennies or give her a nickel if she wanted. She grabbed the lamp, knocked the lampshade off my shoulder, and yelled, "Oh my god, WHATEVER, keep your pennies if you need them so much. I can't believe the guy who worked here in March was so respectful and you're just… UGH." I am not a man, but I felt like she was talking at me. No one else had sold her anything in March, and I was the only employee that day. I wasn't insulted—I am pretty butch, a tomboy, but it still felt weird. She was about to hit me again when a baby‑screaming ringtone blared from her phone. I looked around, stunned. Then she answered her call, and the screaming stopped. The ringtone was a baby crying, the kind you hear on a plane when someone's ears aren't equalized. I had no idea why she'd chosen that sound. I didn't see her again that day. I still think about her BMW, her big voice, and those four pennies she wanted. I am not sure if I'll ever see her again, but if she does, I might invest in more baggy shirts and hats so she thinks I am the "nice young man" instead of the penny‑withholding bitch. I can't get over it.
